messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Firefighter
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 40

He is 34, a married European man who has spent most of his adult life running toward danger. Before the war zone, he works as a firefighter, and the work suits something steady in him: the routines, the teamwork, the way training narrows fear into action. He is used to smoke, alarms, burned metal, the sight of people on the worst day of their lives. When he volunteers as a relief worker during a leave period, he tells himself it is simply the same instinct in a different setting—help where help is needed, carry what you can, keep moving.

At first, he experiences the war zone through tasks. He unloads medical supplies, helps move families into temporary shelters, carries children wrapped in dusty blankets, and checks pulse and breathing with the practical hands of someone who has seen injury before. He sleeps lightly but tells himself everyone does there. The sounds are constant—distant shelling, generators, shouting, dogs, the thud of helicopters. He notices the smell most: fuel, sewage, blood, hot concrete. What unsettles him is not one dramatic scene at first but the accumulation of them, one after another, with no time to absorb any of it.

The moment that stays with him happens late in the afternoon during what had seemed like a lull. He is helping evacuate civilians from a damaged apartment block when the second strike hits nearby. He remembers the pressure before the sound, a force that lifts dust into his mouth and nose and turns the air white. Then screaming. Part of the stairwell collapses. He and another worker crawl toward where they last saw a mother and her son. He can hear the boy crying, then coughing, then nothing. He digs with his hands until his fingernails split. He knows, even while he is digging, that they are losing time. Someone is shouting for him to move because the building may come down again, but he cannot leave. Later he is pulled away. He remembers looking down and realizing his gloves are gone and his bare hands are slick with someone else’s blood and plaster. He cannot clearly recall how long he remains there. What he carries home is the image of a small red shoe half buried in gray dust.

He returns home expecting relief, but ordinary life feels unreal and offensively intact. His wife picks him up from the airport, and he holds her too tightly, then goes quiet on the drive home. In the first weeks, he tells her pieces of what happened in a flat, almost professional tone, as if giving an incident summary after a fire. But his body tells a different story. At night he jerks awake drenched in sweat, already sitting upright before he fully knows where he is. Sometimes he has the sensation that the bedroom walls are not walls at all but unstable concrete, and he has to turn on the light to orient himself. His wife learns not to touch him suddenly from sleep because once he swung his arm out before recognizing her, and the shame of that sits heavily on him.

Back at the station, he is competent, but no longer easy. The tones drop and his heart punches hard in his chest before his mind catches up. Certain calls—collapsed structures, pediatric injuries, heavy dust—pull him somewhere else. He becomes intensely focused, almost rigid, and afterward he needs a few extra minutes by the truck, helmet off, breathing through his mouth. He starts scanning every scene for secondary danger, unable to trust that the first disaster is the only one. His crew notices he startles at sharp metallic bangs. He laughs it off, says he is tired.

At home, he becomes both watchful and absent. He checks the locks repeatedly before bed. In restaurants he chooses seats facing the door and tracks exits without meaning to. Fireworks one weekend send him straight to the floor of the garden before he can stop himself; afterward he is furious with himself and embarrassed in front of the neighbors. He avoids news footage, then compulsively reads updates late at night on his phone, as if vigilance could undo what happened. He has stopped playing music in the car because certain percussion sounds remind him of artillery. He keeps seeing the buried shoe at odd moments—while folding laundry, while tying his own boots at the station, while watching his wife leave her shoes by the door.

His wife says he is home but not fully with her. He knows what she means. He loves her, but he feels partitioned off, as if there is a sealed room inside him where the war remains ongoing. She asks simple questions—How was your shift? What are you thinking about?—and he says “nothing” because the true answer feels impossible to translate. Guilt runs under much of it: guilt that he left alive, guilt that he could not reach the boy, guilt that he came back to a clean kitchen and hot water and a wife who still expects a future. He tells himself he should be stronger; after all, he is a firefighter, someone trained to function in chaos. But the chaos now follows him into quiet places, and quiet itself no longer feels safe.
